Severity was assessed by two dermatologists.

So, in ninety seconds. Two hundred and forty adults with mild to moderate plaque psoriasis were enrolled at four centers, between March and July. Half were treated once a day, half twice a day, for twelve weeks. Our main outcome was the change in severity from baseline, measured at week twelve, and it was assessed by two dermatologists who did not know which schedule the patient had been given. Now, the headline. Severity fell in both groups, and the difference between them was small. It was not significant. What was significant, and honestly what I did not expect, was adherence. Seventy-one per cent of the once-daily group used the treatment as prescribed, against forty-eight per cent of the other group. And better adherence was associated with a better outcome, in both arms. I want to be careful with that sentence, because it is not the same as saying that adherence caused the outcome. We did not design the study to answer that. The limitation you should have in mind is the follow-up. Twelve weeks is short for a condition that comes and goes over years, and we cannot tell you anything about what happens after the course ends. Thank you.

People ask me what gets a paper sent back most often, and they expect me to say the statistics, or the English. It is neither. It is the conclusion. The study shows that two things appeared together, and then the last paragraph says that one of them caused the other. That is not a small slip. It is a different claim, and the study was never built to support it. So we send it back, and nine times out of ten the authors soften the sentence and the paper is fine. The second thing is the word significant. Authors use it as if it meant large, and it does not. It means unlikely to be the result of chance. A difference can be perfectly significant and far too small for any patient to notice, and when that happens somebody has to say so, in the paper, in plain words. And what do I like to see? A limitations section written by people who found the weakness themselves. When the authors name the problem before a reviewer has to point it out, I trust the rest of the paper more, not less. It reads like somebody who was actually looking.

Two hundred and forty adults with plaque psoriasis were enrolled at four centers. Severity was assessed at baseline and again at week twelve. The difference between the two schedules was small and it was not significant. Adherence was much better in the once-daily group. Better adherence was associated with a better outcome. The authors conclude that once a day is enough.
